newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan tells ADB that aid may have to take backseat.
newsitem.headline: Japan tells ADB that aid may have to take backseat.

text.p: Japan, the world's biggest aid donor, on Sunday signalled that budgetary constraints at home may make it less generous with aid to poor nations.
In a speech to the annual meeting of the Asian Development Bank (ADB), Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka bluntly stated Japan was no longer the richest of the world's rich nations.
"Since our fiscal situation is the worst among industrial countries, fiscal reform is among our top priorities," Mitsuzuka told the meeting's opening session in the southern Japanese city of Fukuoka.
He said Japan in recent years had a proud record of giving the most development aid of any industrialised nation, particularly to Asia, despite enormous fiscal pressures at home.
But aid was now under threat because Japan's own economy needed massive amounts spent on restructuring to make Tokyo competitive in the world once more.
"When implementing fiscal structural reforms, however, Official Development Aid (ODA) cannot be exempted from our effort to cut down on expenditure," Mitsuzuka said.
The Japanese economy has been in a slump since its asset "bubble" burst in 1990. It has struggled to find a recover path and a way through the burden of massive bank debts.
Since 1991, Japan has topped the list of donor countries in terms of money spent, although it has fallen back in the rankings of aid as a percentage of gross national product (GNP).
Mitsuzuka's message was one the ADB feared it would hear and added to the existing "donor fatigue" in the 56-member group that provides development assistance to the Asia-Pacific region.
Tokyo's official aid grew in leaps and bounds from the late 1970's as resource-poor Japan strengthened friendships with resource-rich developing nations.
In recent years, donor nations like the United States, and now Japan, have urged the newly-wealthy nations of Asia to foot more of the ADB bill.

Mitsuzuka also pointed a finger at the ADB itself saying the bank needed to carry out its objectives of helping poor nations in a more efficient and effective manner and in greater coordination with the private sector.
"The increased sense of ownership on the part of the borrowers will also be indispensable," he added.
The Japanese finance minister stressed a mind-over-matter approach to the changing role of the bank, saying the ADB should promote intellectual exchange.
He said the ADB Institute, scheduled to open in Tokyo later this year, will explore new development philosophies and basic strategies for the 21st century.
"The challenge that needs to be addressed by the bank is diverse," Mitsuzuka said.
